AGO.text: Mbanza Kongo, on a plateau at 570 m, was the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, one of the largest states in Southern Africa from the 14th to the 19th century.

BDI.text: In Burundi, the royal drum dance blends powerful, synchronized drumming with dancing, heroic poetry and songs. The drums, always an odd number, surround a central drum.

BEN.text: From 1625 to 1900, twelve kings ruled the Kingdom of Abomey. Almost all of them built their palaces inside the same earthen-walled enclosure.

BFA.text: The Loropeni ruins, with their imposing stone walls, are at least 1,000 years old. They recall the gold trade across the Sahara.

BWA.text: Seretse Khama, born in Serowe, was the first president of Botswana (1966-1980), after the former Bechuanaland became independent.

CAF.text: Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic, is home to the University of Bangui (1969), the National School of Arts (1966) and scientific and technological research institutes.

CIV.text: Grand-Bassam, the first capital of Côte d'Ivoire, was a major port and trading centre. It drew people from all over Africa, from Europe and from the Levant.

CMR.text: In Cameroon, the Bamum king Njoya invented a writing system around 1895, opened schools to teach it and commissioned a printing press.

COD.text: Congolese rumba, a music and dance of cities in the DR Congo and Congo, comes from an old dance called nkumba ('waist' in Kikongo). UNESCO listed it in 2021.

COG.text: The Equator crosses the Republic of the Congo, just north of the town of Liranga. Brazzaville is a major port on the Congo River.

COM.text: In Comoros, Comorian (Shikomor), French and Arabic are official languages. Shingazidja, spoken on Grande Comore, appears in the weekly newspaper Al Watwan.

CPV.text: Cidade Velha, on the island of Santiago, was called Ribeira Grande. You can still see two churches, a royal fortress and part of the original street layout.

DJI.text: In Djibouti, a railway has linked the port to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, since 1917. The port serves as a trading point between Ethiopia and the Red Sea.

DZA.text: The Kasbah of Algiers had a great influence on architecture and town planning in North Africa, Andalusia and sub-Saharan Africa in the 16th and 17th centuries.

EGY.text: The pyramid fields from Giza to Dahshur surround Memphis, capital of the Old Kingdom. In ancient times, the site was counted among the Seven Wonders of the World.

ERI.text: Asmara, the capital of Eritrea, stands at over 2,000 m above sea level and is famous for its modernist architecture.

ETH.text: At Lalibela, in the heart of Ethiopia, eleven medieval churches were carved out of living rock in a mountainous region.

GAB.text: Libreville is Gabon's centre of education: Omar Bongo University dates from 1970, alongside research institutes in geology, mining and agronomy.

GHA.text: Near Kumasi, the traditional Asante buildings, made of earth, wood and straw, are the last remains of the great Asante civilization of the 18th century.

GIN.text: In Guinea, the Sosso-Bala, a balafon kept at Nyagassola, has carried epic poems for centuries, above all the Sunjata epic. A family of griots teaches how to play it.

GMB.text: Along the River Gambia, over 1,000 monuments, including circles of laterite pillars, form a sacred landscape created over more than 1,500 years.

GNB.text: In Guinea-Bissau, tides reach up to 100 km inland. Their brackish water is used to irrigate rice paddies called bolanhas.

GNQ.text: In Equatorial Guinea, Spanish, French and Portuguese are official languages. People also speak languages such as Fang and Bubi.

KEN.text: Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o published 'Weep Not, Child' in 1964, the first major novel in English by an East African. He later wrote in Kikuyu.

LBR.text: In Liberia, the Vai people invented their own alphabet, a script created right there.

LBY.text: Cyrene, founded by Greeks from the island of Thera, stayed a great capital until the earthquake of 365. A thousand years of history is written into its ruins.

LSO.text: In Lesotho, the Highlands Water Project includes dams, reservoirs, tunnels and a hydroelectric power station. The Katse Dam was completed in 1997.

MAR.text: Ait-Ben-Haddou, near Ouarzazate, is a ksar: earthen houses crowded together behind high walls reinforced by corner towers.

MDG.text: The Royal Hill of Ambohimanga is the cradle of the kingdom and the dynasty that made Madagascar a modern state, recognised since 1817.

MLI.text: In Djenné, nearly 2,000 traditional houses have survived. They are built on mounds called toguere to protect them from seasonal floods.

MOZ.text: In Mozambique, Chopi orchestras bring together five to thirty wooden xylophones, called timbila, fitted with gourd resonators.

MRT.text: Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata in Mauritania were founded in the 11th-12th centuries on the caravan routes. These trading towns became centres of culture and thought.

MUS.text: In Mauritius, Creole is the common language and schools encourage multilingualism: many Mauritians speak two or more languages.

MWI.text: In Malawi, William Kamkwamba built a windmill from scrap materials as a teenager to power his family's home. He wrote a book about it.

NAM.text: In Namibia, the Twyfelfontein engravings, at least 2,000 years old, form one of the largest concentrations of rock art in Africa.

NER.text: Agadez, the 'gateway to the desert', is a caravan trade city. Its 27 m minaret, built entirely of mud brick, is the tallest of its kind in the world, says UNESCO.

NGA.text: Wole Soyinka, a Nigerian author born in Abeokuta, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, a first for a writer from sub-Saharan Africa.

RWA.text: Intore is a Rwandan dance performed by a troupe, to the rhythm of drums, with songs and poems. Schools and universities organise training sessions.

SDN.text: Between the Nile and the Atbara, Meroe was the heartland of the Kingdom of Kush. Its remains include pyramids, temples and major water-management works.

SEN.text: Poet Léopold Sédar Senghor published 'Chants d'ombre' in 1945. Senegal's first president, he joined the Académie française in 1984, its first African member.

SLE.text: The name Sierra Leone comes from the Portuguese Serra Lyoa, "Lion Mountains", given by an explorer to the hills around Freetown harbour.

SOM.text: Somalia is the easternmost country of Africa, on the Horn of Africa. The frankincense tree (Boswellia) grows in its northern mountains.

SSD.text: Juba, capital of South Sudan, is a Nile river port and a road hub towards Uganda, Kenya and the DR Congo. The University of Juba was founded there in 1975.

STP.text: In São Tomé and Príncipe, people speak Portuguese and three creoles: Sãotomense, Angolar and Principense.

SWZ.text: At Ngwenya in Eswatini, people were already mining red ochre and sparkling haematite at least 42,000 years ago: one of the oldest mines in the world.

SYC.text: In Seychelles, on Praslin island, the Vallée de Mai is home to the coco de mer, whose seed is the largest in the plant kingdom.

TCD.text: Near Lake Chad, the medieval Sao culture left works in terracotta and bronze, unearthed in the 1950s along the Logone and Chari rivers.

TGO.text: In Koutammakou, in north-eastern Togo, the Batammariba build mud tower-houses called takienta, grouped in villages with springs and ceremonial spaces.

TUN.text: Dougga, built on a height overlooking a fertile plain, was the capital of a Libyco-Punic state. Its impressive Roman ruins can still be visited.

TZA.text: Kilwa Kisiwani, a Swahili city in Tanzania, minted its own coins and traded with Arabia, India and China between the 13th and 16th centuries.

UGA.text: In Kampala, Makerere University began in 1922 as a technical school and became a university in 1970. For many years it was East Africa's only higher-education institution.

ZAF.text: In South Africa, the Vredefort Dome is the scar of a meteorite impact about 2 billion years old, one of the oldest and largest known on Earth.

ZMB.text: In Zambia, the Kalela dance, born in Luapula Province and taken up by miners, is danced in lines moving forwards and backwards, singing to the beat of three drums.

ZWE.text: In Zimbabwe, the stone city of Great Zimbabwe, built between 1100 and 1450, gave the country its name: in Shona, "zimbabwe" means "house of stone".
